Title: The Tile Look, Without the Grout
Scope: Primary suite wet room walls, color-matched to the tile spec
Description: Print-featured wet room: the designer's tile aesthetic delivered in non-porous colorback glass — zero grout, 60–70% less cleaning.
Challenge: The designer had fallen in love with a specific tile aesthetic for the wet room walls — but the homeowner, experienced with luxury home maintenance, was adamant about not living with grout. Porous grout joints harbor mold and mildew in wet environments and never stop demanding upkeep.
Approach: Rather than abandon the design, we fabricated tempered colorback glass panels digitally color-matched to the exact tile shade — the aesthetic the designer loved, in a non-porous surface that meets Glass Association of North America performance standards. Installation was single-stage and fit the construction schedule without tile's multi-step process.
Result: The finished wet room delivers the designer's vision with none of the maintenance: non-porous glass requires 60–70% less cleaning time and chemicals than tile-and-grout systems, and there's no grout to crack, discolor, or generate builder callbacks. The completed bathroom was later featured in print editorials.
Quote: I will not deal with grout in my shower.
QuoteWho: The homeowner's brief — honored in full

Title: Privacy that didn't look like a compromise
Systems: 3/8″ grey-tinted tempered · dual-swing pivot · matte black hardware
Description: Grey-tinted enclosure giving a teenager privacy in a shared bath — recommended over satin-etch because it reads as design, not a fix.
Challenge: In a five-bedroom new build, the boys' rooms shared a bathroom — no ensuite in the plan. The teenage son wanted more privacy than a clear enclosure gives, and his mom brought the request to the build team looking for recommendations, not products.
Approach: We recommended grey-tinted glass over the usual satin-etch. Same privacy, different message: frosted glass reads as a utility fix, while grey reads as a design decision — edgier, more modern, and right at home with the house's matte black finishes. Fabricated as a two-panel inline enclosure in 3/8-inch tempered grey glass with a 28-inch pivot door that swings both in and out.
Result: Set on the standard one-week measure-to-install timeline, about two days on site. The family loved it — and that word came back through the builder, which counts double.
Quote: Builders don't usually call about a shower. When she called to say the family loved it — that's a big deal.

Title: Grey mirror in a designer's own home
Systems: 1/4″ grey mirror · precision cutouts for wall-mounted faucet
Client: Interior designer — her own home, first of two
Timeline: Sequenced over several weeks with the full sub team
Description: Statement grey mirror in an entertaining-first powder bath — noticeable, without taking focus from the art.
Challenge: This was the first home we did for an interior designer — her own place in Southlake, about 10,000 square feet. The entry powder bath mattered to her because she likes to entertain, and that's the room guests actually see. She wanted it to make a statement, and she wanted the mirror to be different — but she was also planning artwork for the room, and we didn't want the mirror taking too much away from that focal point.
Approach: Grey mirror got it done on both counts: different enough to notice, quiet enough that the art stays the focus. One panel, roughly 60 by 84 inches at a quarter inch thick, running from the countertop up toward the eleven-foot ceiling, with cutouts for the wall-mounted faucet. Cutouts make any piece of glass more fragile, especially at a quarter inch — these sat far enough from the edges to keep the piece manageable, and Dion is meticulous about his measurements. Years of measuring colorback glass will do that. Fit wasn't a problem.
Result: The mirror went in as part of the larger build — a lot of moving parts, several weeks, a layered team effort by all the subs. The room came out the way she wanted: the mirror gets noticed, the art keeps the room. And she hired us again for her family's next home before they moved out of state.
Quote: Designers see everyone's work up close. Getting picked for her own home told us where we stand.

Title: The kitchen everyone ends up in
Scope: Full backsplash run — panels up to 12 ft, seams hidden at the vent hood
Systems: Colorback glass — exact match to the island's accent color
Client: Builder partner, multi-year Top Builder — her parents' home
Description: A dual-tone green backsplash matched to the island's accent — built for a Top Builder's own parents and a kitchen full of grandkids. Seams hidden at the vent hood.
Challenge: This one was for our builder partner's own parents. She's a Little Rock builder who's been named Top Builder there multiple years running — and this was her mom and dad's new build, so we knew we had to kick it up a notch. They're retired, and they weren't exactly sizing down. It's a big family that always congregates at their house: lots of kids, lots of grandkids, everyone cooking, everyone serving themselves around an oversized island. With that much traffic, grout behind the counters was going to be a losing battle. And this couple likes color — being able to choose their color mattered.
Approach: They chose a dark green with blue undertones — a dual-tone color that can lean blue or lean green depending on the light — matched exactly to the accent color on the base of their island, so the backsplash and the island tie the room together. Measuring for these is an art form: custom cabinets in luxury homes mean you're working down to the millimeter, and installing in a finished house — freshly painted walls, freshly painted cabinets, brand-new appliances — means a tight fit with nothing you can afford to scratch. Glass panels run up to about twelve feet, so on a long counter you have to be crafty about the seams. Here, they sit at the cabinet lines flanking the vent hood: the hood holds your eye, the symmetry does the rest, and you just don't see them. We use that one a lot. Cutouts are their own discipline — every outlet, every notch under the cabinets — and where the color allows it, we back-paint glass outlet and switch covers to match exactly, so even the switches disappear into the run.
Result: The family was thrilled — and then they asked the question everyone asks when we present colorback glass: why don't more people choose this? Why don't people know about it? Since people always want to know what it costs, the honest answer: more than tile, less than marble or granite. The difference lives in the cutouts, the precision fit, and a paint made to stand up to heat and cold. You get what you pay for.
Quote: Why don't people know about this?
QuoteWho: The homeowners — the question every colorback client asks

Title: Steam after a day on the lake
Scope: Steam-rated corner enclosure with operable transom
Systems: 3/8″ tempered · bulb seals on door and transom · matte black hardware
Timeline: An hour past our usual area — for repeat clients, we drive
Description: A steam-rated enclosure in a small-but-luxe lake cabin — recovery after a day of water skiing, warmth over the holidays. Went in clean, no callbacks.

It came through a builder partner we work with all the time, about an hour past our usual install area; for loyal clients, we make the drive. The brief was steam after a day on the lake: water skiing is tough on the body, and the shower doubles as recovery — and as a warm luxury when the family gathers there over the holidays.

The transom is operable — we always suggest that, because, honestly, how often does the steam feature actually get used? Most days it's just a great shower, and an operable transom lets it breathe. The cabin was a new build, so everything was plumb and straight — for the moment — and the enclosure went in clean.

Title: Even the guest bath is a jewel box
Scope: Full-height framed steam enclosure — part of a whole-home glass and mirror package
Systems: 3/8″ Starphire · polished nickel framing · waterproofed ceiling
Client: Interior designer — found us through our website
Timeline: About three weeks — framed work earns a longer schedule, by agreement
Description: A full-height steam enclosure framed in polished nickel — the Italian art-deco look done right, in Starphire against dramatic veined marble. Every anchor a held breath.
Challenge: An interior designer found us through our website for her townhome near downtown Dallas — a complete remodel, taken down to the studs. We did the glass and mirror through the whole house, but the room worth telling is not the primary bath. It's the guest bath, wrapped floor to ceiling in dramatic veined marble — and the designer was deep in an Italian art-deco moment. Here's the thing about that look: in the era it comes from, frameless glass didn't exist. Showers were framed in polished metal, like everything else worth looking at. So our signature frameless approach would have been the wrong answer, and we knew it.
Approach: A fully framed steam enclosure, run all the way to the waterproofed ceiling with a glass band across the top — a little glass architecture, banded like the era demanded. The framing did double duty: anchored to the marble walls, it carried most of the stability, so we weren't hunting studs across the ceiling. The glass is 3/8-inch Starphire — low-iron, almost invisible — because with marble like that, the glass's job is to get out of the way. The frame is polished nickel, not chrome — chrome patinas quickly in a wet area; nickel holds its finish and runs a touch warmer against the stone. No transom — in a guest bath, the steam feature is an occasional luxury. Every anchor into that marble was a held breath: drilling stone takes special bits and a steady hand — slip and you scratch it, crack it, chip it. A costly mistake, sure, but that's not really why we were careful. Who would want to damage something so beautiful?
Result: This one didn't run on our usual one-week shower timeline — framed work takes longer, and the designer agreed the three weeks were worth it. She was there with us every step, a real partner. The enclosure went in clean, the marble untouched except where it was meant to be touched. And when her next project came — a large home in Highland Park — she brought us with her.
Quote: Who would want to damage something so beautiful?

Title: Clean enough for a surgeon
Scope: Two 4′ × 8′ colorback panels · frameless enclosure · vanity mirror
Systems: Grey-blue colorback matched to the designer's palette · hardware cutouts
Client: GC partner — full commercial remodel, taken to the studs
Timeline: Daytime work — doctor operating from another suite
Description: Grey-blue colorback in a surgeon's private shower — no grout, sprayable with alcohol — plus a consultation pocket door and custom mirrors through the suite. One remodel became three years of work.

Title: A wine room in full daylight
Scope: 4 slim-profile aluminum-framed panels — one an 11-ft full-height door
Timeline: Coordinated with the exterior glazing sub
Description: A UV-protected glass wine room in full daylight — an entertaining room, not an aging cellar, off the dining room with the golf course beyond.
Challenge: This wine room sits right off the dining room with glass on two sides: ours on the inside, floor-to-ceiling windows on the corner, overlooking the golf course. The builder is one of our regular partners — they build beautiful, award-winning homes — and this was meant to be a dramatic focal point the family uses year-round. The honest conversation up front: a glass room in full daylight is the opposite of a wine cave. This was actually our second one — the first was a temperature-controlled room inside a sunroom — so we'd already worked through those considerations with a builder and designer before.
Approach: The room is climate controlled and UV protected. It's an entertaining and display room, definitely not an aging cellar, and everything was specced around that honesty. We did all the interior work: four slim-profile aluminum-framed panels, one of them a full-height eleven-foot door on pivot hinges, so a door that size opens effortlessly. The channel system is one we use often in small commercial, and we meet stone all the time in storefronts — so landing the frames against the stacked stone was well within our wheelhouse: flashing and sealed channels between the stone and the frame, for good measure, even with the exterior glazing carrying its own.

As for the builder's reaction — it's the nicest thing anyone has ever said about our glazing, and too generous to put in writing. We'll just say we heard it, and that we keep working with them regularly, on their luxury homes and their custom ones too.
Quote: The nicest thing a builder has ever said about our work — we'll keep the exact words to ourselves.

Title: A staircase that looks like it's floating
Scope: 241.5 sq ft · 15 panels — stair flights + both loft runs
Timeline: Templated per panel · set in about a day, two-man crew
Description: Half a ton of near-invisible low-iron glass wrapping a floating stair and loft — set by a two-man crew in about a day.
Challenge: The ask on this one was simple to say and hard to do: make the staircase look like it's floating. Floating oak treads in a two-story foyer, glass climbing the stair and wrapping both sides of the loft above it — and the glass had to disappear. We came in through a stair contractor new to us who builds massive homes. We weren't there at the drawing stage, but on site, while the build gets finalized, we have a lot of input.
Approach: Starphire glass is what makes it work: half-inch tempered, low-iron — standard glass reads green at that thickness, and Starphire is almost invisible. You can tell. Fifteen panels, 241.5 square feet, a little over half a ton of glass. Every panel gets measured individually, and a template made and numbered so there's no confusion. We learned that lesson a long time ago — templates are a small expense in the long run, and worth every penny.
Result: Two men set it in about a day. The templates and adjustable standoffs kept the hours down — measure twice — and that kind of install speed is another reason builders choose Eridion. The staircase floats, the glass disappears, and the stair contractor has already slotted us for their next two homes.
Quote: The ask was to make the staircase float. I think we read the assignment.

Title: Five hundred pounds, one pinky
Scope: 8′ × 8′ center-pivot glass door with a sidelite filling the opening
Systems: 1/2″ clear tempered · fully framed · center-pivot hinges, special-ordered from Germany
Client: Veteran-owned gym — referred by an employee of one of our builder partners
Timeline: Three weeks for the hinges to cross the Atlantic — worth it
Description: An 8×8 center-pivot door in half-inch glass — 500 pounds that move with a pinky. Muffles the class noise without choking the traffic. The gym changed hands; the door stayed.
Challenge: A veteran-owned gym in Little Rock found us the best way there is: a gym member who worked for one of our builder partners told the owner to give us a call. The problem was an opening — no door at all — between the class space and a hallway that led to the smoothie bar and two recovery rooms. Classes and clanging weights poured noise straight down that hall. But a regular set of double doors would have choked the traffic; the way the space flowed, with people moving between classes, smoothies, and recovery, swinging doors would slow everyone down all day to solve a problem that only existed during class.
Approach: We suggested a center-pivot door: a single eight-by-eight-foot panel of half-inch glass that rotates on pivot points at top and bottom, with a slim sidelite filling the rest of the opening. The physics is the whole trick — the pivots carry the entire weight of the door on its axis, so all five hundred pounds move with a pinky finger. Parked open, it disappears and the opening flows like there's no door at all; one easy push and the class is behind glass. The half-inch thickness matters twice: it keeps a panel that size from bowing, and the sheer mass of the glass is what muffles the noise — this was never meant to be soundproof, just to take the edge off the clanging, and it does. Fully framed, so the edges can't chip and the panel is protected from shattering. The hinges were a special order from Germany — three weeks in transit; we've since found a U.S. supplier, so the next one ships faster. Setting a five-hundred-pound panel is a leverage game, and the crew has it down to a science — but the owner, a genuinely muscular guy, wanted to help anyway. OSHA rules don't allow it, so he stood close behind, just in case. That's the kind of client he was.
Result: He got exactly the cool vibe he wanted — at the opening, we stood back and watched everyone ogling the door. The gym itself didn't make it, which genuinely made us sad; the owner was passionate about the place. But here's the part that says everything about the work: the space is an indoor golf-simulator business now, and the new owners kept the door. Tenants change. The right answer for a space stays.
Quote: The pivots carry all five hundred pounds — you can move it with your pinky.

Title: The basketball hoop on the other side of the wall
Scope: Roughly 100 feet of mirror wall — full demo of the failed wall, new framed install
Systems: Safety-backed mirror · framed mounting with room to flex
Client: Facility owner — the lead physical therapist, found us online
Timeline: 14–16-hour controlled demo, then the new wall
Description: Mirrors kept cracking and nobody knew why — until we looked at the basketball hoop on the other side of the shared wall. Safety backing and a framed, flex-tolerant mount fixed it.
Challenge: The owner of a physical-therapy and athletic-performance gym in DFW found us online with a mystery: the mirrors along one wall of his training floor kept cracking, and he couldn't figure out why. We could. On the other side of that wall was a basketball training facility — with a hoop mounted directly against the shared wall. Every drill, every rebound, every body hitting the floor sent vibration through the studs, and mirror glued rigid to a wall that moves is going to lose that fight every time. Nobody had ever looked at the problem from the other side of the wall.
Approach: Before anything new could go up, the old wall had to come down — and pulling glued, cracked mirror off a wall is the half of this trade nobody photographs for the portfolio. Fourteen to sixteen hours in full protective kit: face shields, gauntlets, coveralls, steel-toed boots. The crew sawed each panel cleanly off its adhesive, cracking glass only when they chose to, never by accident — then went back and chipped the dried mastic off the wall until there was a flat, true surface to build on. The new wall got two upgrades. Safety backing — a film on the back of the glass, so if a mirror ever does break, the pieces stick to the backing instead of coming down on someone mid-workout; in a room full of athletes, that's not optional. And framed mounting: the frame carries the mirror's weight and gives the glass a little room to move when the wall gets jostled, instead of holding it rigid against every vibration. Still glued, still solid — just no longer fighting the basketball court next door.
Result: We never got another call — and in mirror work, that's the review. The phone rings when something cracks. Gym mirrors live a hard life anywhere; the fix was never mirrors that can't break, it was mirrors that stop breaking for no reason and stay safe if they ever do. Athletic facilities have been steady work for us since — right now we're building out mirror walls for a large fitness chain across Arkansas.
Quote: Glass glued rigid to a wall that moves is going to lose that fight. Give it a frame and a little room to flex.

Title: One web search, then storefronts across DFW
Scope: Storefront + interior glass for seven-plus retail locations over four years
Systems: Aluminum storefront · bronze & smoky-grey mirrors · shelving & partitions
Client: Retail GC — national eyewear brand program
Timeline: Storefront up in ~2 days · interior glass around the other trades
Description: Seven-plus brand storefronts for the same GC across DFW — each brand's standards held, from bronze mirror to smoky grey, storefront to interior glass.
Challenge: Early in Eridion's history, a general contractor found us through a web search. He held the buildout contract for a national eyewear company with several retail brands under it — stores in shopping centers and malls across DFW, each one on a hard opening date. On a brand program like this, the specs arrive settled: the national office has already negotiated materials with its own vendors, and everything ships straight to the site. That's a different rhythm from the commercial and residential work where we're advising on glass and methods from the start — here, the skill is taking what procurement sends and turning it into a finished store, correctly, on schedule, brand after brand.
Approach: After the first few stores, the brand standards stopped being a puzzle. You learn which brand runs bronze mirror and which runs smoky grey. You learn which stores take a full interior package — mirrors, glass shelving, partitions — and which are storefront-only. You learn what changes when there's an optometrist in the store and a physician's requirements enter the drawings. Once we knew each brand's differentiators, we could move fast: a storefront goes up in about two days, interior glass in one or two more, sequenced around the brake metal delivery and the other subs. Our installers are skilled in both commercial and residential work — you don't find that often. The store pictured went in around Christmas, in the middle of one of the busiest shopping and entertainment centers in the area — one level, no back corridor, which meant carrying glass by hand a few hundred yards, weaving through holiday crowds, load after load. That was the hard part. The install itself went smoothly.
Result: Seven-plus storefronts for the same contractor over four years, all across DFW, from “Opening Soon” vinyl to open doors. When the next store comes up, they know who to call — and they keep calling.
Quote: Every brand has a standard, and they're trusting you to hold it — store after store, across the whole market.

Title: The backsplash they ordered twice
Scope: Matte colorback kitchenette backsplash — a 12-ft run with a 3-ft return, within a whole-office glass package
Systems: Satin-etched colorback glass · matte face out, gloss to the wall · near-black
Client: Builder partner — their own office, a 13-person team
Timeline: The office set the schedule; the backsplash itself goes up in about an hour
Description: Matte colorback in a builder's own break room — reads like a chalkboard, cleans like glass, doubles as the office message board. Re-ordered when they moved offices.
Challenge: This is a builder partner's own office in Little Rock — a thirteen-person team, and we did the glass throughout. But the interesting part is how the kitchenette happened: they treated their new office like a model home and asked us what we wanted to showcase in it. Any sub who's ever wished a builder would just let them show what they can do knows what an invitation that is. We chose something most people haven't seen: matte colorback glass.
Approach: Colorback glass is usually glossy — that's the look people know from our kitchens and wet rooms. This is the same product, flipped: satin-etched glass, back-painted, with the gloss face against the wall carrying the color and the soft etched face outward. The finish reads matte — near-black here, quiet against the dark cabinets — but it behaves exactly like glass, because it is glass: no grout, wipes clean with window cleaner, vinegar, or alcohol. A twelve-foot run with a three-foot return, cutouts for every outlet and switch. Then the backsplash grew a second job. The first time I saw the matte finish I thought: that looks like a chalkboard. It evolved from there — the team started writing on it with neon dry-erase markers, and the break-room backsplash became the office message board. Wipes clean, obviously. It's glass.
Result: The whole office ran on a construction schedule, but the backsplash itself went up in about an hour — colorback is a fast install once the measuring is done right. The real verdict came later: the team grew, the builder moved to a bigger office, and they asked us to build the same backsplash again. It's already on the wall in the new space. A builder sees every product on the market — and when they moved, this is the one they took with them.
Quote: When they moved offices, they asked for the same backsplash again. That's the whole review.
